name: Matrixyl

lead: Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4) is a cosmetic peptide used in serums, creams and eye products to soften wrinkles and fine lines, including around the eyes. It was launched in 2000 by the French ingredient maker Sederma.

The peptide is a fragment related to collagen breakdown that acts as a messenger, and in cell studies it stimulates production of type I and III collagen and other matrix components. A palmitic acid chain is attached to help it cross the skin's lipid barrier. Studies by the supplier and by independent groups have been published, and many human studies are small or compare it with other peptides.

paras: It is applied as a daily serum or cream, often combined with other peptides, retinoids and moisturizers, and judged over weeks to months. Results depend on the formulation and how much reaches the target skin layer.
It is considered low-risk, with rare irritation, and is freely sold as a cosmetic. Reported effects are modest.

angle.text: Matrixyl is a cosmetic peptide used in serums and creams to soften wrinkles and fine lines, including around the eyes. It signals skin cells to make collagen, so skin can look slightly firmer. Small studies, many manufacturer-linked, have measured modest wrinkle changes.

lead: Matrixyl is the trade name of palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Pal-KTTKS), a small signal peptide used in anti-wrinkle creams, serums and eye products. People use it to soften the look of fine lines and to firm skin: the idea is that the peptide, a fragment resembling a piece of collagen, signals skin fibroblasts to make more collagen and other matrix components, so lines look shallower and skin looks smoother over weeks of daily use.[1][2][3] It is the best-known example of a cosmetic matrikine peptide and appears in many leave-on products.[1][4]

The ingredient was launched in 2000 by the French cosmetic-ingredient maker Sederma SAS, and its INCI name changed from palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 to pentapeptide-4 in 2006.[1] A related blend, Matrixyl 3000, combines palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7.[5] In looksmaxxing skin threads it is discussed as a topical alternative to copper-peptide GHK-Cu and to retinoids for collagen and skin quality.[6]

Research on Pal-KTTKS includes cell studies showing collagen stimulation in fibroblasts, human trials of peptide creams for wrinkles that mix industry-sponsored and independent designs, and materials work on how the lipopeptide self-assembles.[7][8][3][2] A 2026 review concludes that peptide evidence should be read product by product, because many trials are small, short or industry-sponsored and use multi-ingredient formulas.[2]
infobox: Creams, serums, eye products, stretch-mark creams[1][4]

paras: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 is used in anti-wrinkle creams, serums and eye products intended to reduce the appearance of fine lines and improve firmness and texture.[1][3] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, says it is typically used at very low concentrations and appears in more than 200 formulations.[9] A DailyMed label for a stretch-mark cream lists palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 among several peptides, with external-use warnings.[4]

Combinations are common. The Matrixyl 3000 trade blend contains palmitoyl tripeptide-1 (Pal-GHK) and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7.[5] A 2025 in vitro study examined palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 with another peptide and injectable platelet-rich fibrin on dermal fibroblasts.[10] A 2022 study compared a Matrixyl patch with a Matrixyl cream for wound healing.[11]

On looksmax.org a user planning to buy topical GHK-Cu to boost collagen and elasticity asked whether Matrixyl, which he found in a skin looksmaxxing thread, was the better choice; a reply recommended GHK-Cu.[6] A 2013 T Nation poster asked about peptides including TB-500, GHK, Biopeptide EL and Matrixyl in connection with healing times and scarring.[12] In both cases Matrixyl is treated as one of several peptide actives people read about for skin quality.

Matrikines are messenger peptides that regulate cell activity through specific receptors and activate genes involved in extracellular matrix renewal and cell proliferation.[1] KTTKS corresponds to a sequence from type I procollagen and arises from collagen breakdown, and its palmitoylated form is more stable.[13][9] A 2025 review states that it passes into the dermis, binds a cell-surface receptor and boosts collagen types I and III, and may also reduce collagen degradation and regulate hyaluronic acid synthesis in fibroblasts.[3]

Laboratory work shows that C16-KTTKS stimulates collagen production in human dermal and corneal fibroblasts in a concentration-dependent manner, close to the concentration at which it self-assembles into nanotape structures, suggesting the two are related.[7] Researchers have also designed lipopeptide variants carrying cycloalkane chains or carnosine motifs from the KTTKS sequence.[14][15]

The palmitoyl chain, a 16-carbon fatty acid, is added to help the peptide cross the lipid layers of the skin.[1] The 2025 review on skin senescence nevertheless identifies poor membrane permeability as a major drawback for peptides in general, since they are hydrophilic and often large, and notes that delivery is favoured by low molecular weight and positive charge.[3] It describes chemical enhancers, microneedles (tested with this peptide by one group) and nanocarriers such as ethosomes as ways to improve delivery.[3]

A 2026 study characterises how cosmetic actives, including peptides found in Matrixyl 3000, permeate human stratum corneum, and a 2025 study tested glycyrrhizic acid nanomicelles to improve transdermal delivery of palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 as a model signal peptide.[5][16] The 2026 review of aesthetic peptides adds that lipidation, encapsulation and microneedles change skin exposure, which complicates attributing results to the peptide itself.[2]

Pal-KTTKS is a five-residue lipopeptide whose palmitoyl group is attached through an amide bond to the first lysine, with a molar mass of about 802.[1][9][3] Its self-assembly into peptide amphiphile nanostructures has been studied in materials science.[7][14]

A 2025 review reports a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial of 93 women with facial wrinkles using an oil-in-water cream for 12 weeks, in which expert graders saw improved fine lines and overall skin appearance; the same review notes that the concentration is listed inconsistently in its tables.[3] Grokipedia describes the study as a split-face design in women aged 35 to 55 and mentions a 28-day periocular study, but those figures come from an AI-generated summary and are not independently confirmed.[9]

A 2023 randomized double-blind trial in Indonesia compared an acetylhexapeptide-3 cream, a palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 cream and a placebo for crow's feet in 21 women aged 26 to 55, twice daily for eight weeks.[8] Instrument measures of hydration, water loss and elasticity showed no statistically significant differences between groups, and crow's feet grading scores fell in all three groups including placebo. Participants rated the pentapeptide cream "very good" more often, and the authors said larger studies are needed.[8] The study was funded by a company, and no complaints were reported with the pentapeptide cream.[8]

A 2004 randomized trial in 20 breast cancer patients compared a cream containing Matrixyl with CM glucan and hydroxyprolisilan C against Bepanthol lotion during radiotherapy and found no differences in median skin toxicity scores between groups, with mild itchiness and sporadic efflorescences more frequent with the cream.[17] This concerns radiation skin care, not wrinkles.

The 2026 review of aesthetic peptides says controlled human studies report improvements in selected endpoints such as wrinkles, hydration, elasticity, dermal density and pigmentation, but that many trials have small samples, short follow-up, industry sponsorship or multi-ingredient formulations.[2]

Wikipedia has no safety section for palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, and Grokipedia states it is non-sensitizing and non-irritating at reported concentrations.[1][9] The 2025 review reports good tolerance across skin types, including oily and acne-prone skin.[3] In the radiotherapy study, mild itchiness occurred more often with the Matrixyl-containing cream than with the control lotion; in the crow's feet trial, no complaints were recorded with the pentapeptide cream.[17][8]

Researchers have examined analogues of KTTKS for cytotoxicity on fibroblasts and effects on protease activity.[13] A 2026 in-ovo study in chicken embryos reported developmental effects for Argireline and Matrixyl that its authors described as an indication of teratogenic potential; it is an animal-embryo experiment and not a human finding.[18]

Sederma launched palmitoyl pentapeptide as Matrixyl in 2000, and the INCI name changed from pentapeptide-3 to pentapeptide-4 in 2006.[1] Grokipedia says Sederma is now part of Croda.[9] It is widely cited as a prototype of cosmetic signal peptides; Wikipedia lists related molecules including GHK-Cu and palmitoyl tripeptide-38, and later products such as Matrixyl 3000 expanded the line.[1][5] Wikipedia notes that in vitro and in vivo studies of the peptide have been published both by Sederma and by independent groups.[1]

Published human studies are few. They include a double-blind randomized comparison of acetylhexapeptide-3 and palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 creams for crow's feet and a 20-patient randomized trial of a Matrixyl-containing cream during breast radiotherapy that found no difference in skin toxicity versus standard lotion.[8][17] A 12-week trial in 93 women is described in a review.[3] Reviews of aesthetic peptides summarise the clinical evidence and note that much of the mechanistic data are experimental.[2][3] Other research on Matrixyl consists of cell studies, hairless mouse experiments using it as a positive control, and delivery and materials work.[10][16][7][14][19]

lore.intro: In skin looksmaxxing threads on looksmax.org, Matrixyl appears as a topical peptide option compared with GHK-Cu, and it turns up in T Nation questions about healing and scarring.[6][12]

timeline.event: Sederma launches palmitoyl pentapeptide as Matrixyl.[1]
Randomized trial of a Matrixyl-containing cream during breast radiotherapy is published.[17]
The INCI name changes from palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 to pentapeptide-4.[1]
Study shows C16-KTTKS stimulates collagen production in human fibroblasts and links this to its self-assembly.[7]
Studies of KTTKS analogues examine cytotoxicity and protease activity.[13]
Comparison of Matrixyl patch and Matrixyl cream for wound healing.[11]
Randomized trial compares acetylhexapeptide-3 and palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 creams for crow's feet.[8]
Reviews of peptides for skin senescence and tests of nanomicelle delivery of palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 are published.[3][16]
